steps.title: Machine Learning (p158)
steps.prompt: Teach the book's section "Machine Learning (p158)" in dialogue — never lecture more than a few sentences before asking something. Book content to work through: i tiit Through repetition, Maya recognized a pattern: whenever she heard the word ‘cup’, she received the cup itself. This formed an association in her mind between the word ‘cup’ and the object. She learned that the object’s name is ‘cup’. i tiit Shared Shape These images show cups of different sizes, colors, and details. By seeing many different examples, the computer begins to identify the shared shape that makes an object a cup, even when the style, color, or design changes. The ability to identify this shared shape is called pattern recognition. In unsupervised learning, similar objects are grouped together without being told their names. Later, labels such as ‘cups,’ ‘shoes,’ and ‘crayons’ can be added to each group. i tiit Recognized Pattern • Matches the shared shape. • Color does not matter. • Design does not matter. Associations • Label: Cup Model Cup This diagram shows a model of a cup. On the left are the recognized patterns that define a cup. Definitions to land in the student's own words: "One of the fundamental attributes of an intelligent system is —the ability to acquire and use information. Learning involves creating internal links, or associations , between what is already known and new information.

steps.prompt: Run the book's true-or-false check (10 statements). Read each aloud and have the student commit to T or F before you confirm. Statements with the book's answers: 1. Learning is the ability to form and use new associations. — T 2. Pattern recognition allows a system to detect and respond to random or unrelated features. — F 3. Supervised learning uses labeled data. — T 4. Unsupervised learning means the system receives labels in advance and uses them to form associations. — F 5. A model is the internal system that holds the patterns and associations a computer has learned. — T 6. Once a model is created, it can no longer be changed or improved. — F 7. A well-trained model can generalize its learning to identify patterns it has never seen before. — T 10. Repetition helps reinforce associations and improve pattern recognition. tiit — T

steps.title: Talk it through (Activity 1.3)
steps.prompt: Read the narrative and answer the questions below. 1. What type of learning is being used to teach the AI system to identify plants, and how do you know? 2. What features did the model learn to focus on, and which did it learn to ignore? 3. Why is it important to have the model tested on images it had never seen before? 4. Why did the model fail to recognize some of the roses? What was missing? 5. How did the model improve, and what process does this describe? Plant Learning A team of scientists is using machine learning to build a system that can identify different types of plants. At first, they collect thousands of plant images and label each one with its name (e.g., “rose,” “sunflower,” “tulip”). They use these labeled examples to teach the AI system what each plant looks like. Over time, the AI begins to recognize important patterns in the shape of the leaves and petals, while ignoring variations like background color or lighting. Once the model is built, it is tested on a new set of plant images it has never seen before. It correctly identifies many of them but fails to recognize some roses that were photographed from an unusual angle. The scientists examine these mistakes and add more examples showing roses from different angles. The system updates its model and improves its accuracy. Calls of the Wild Scientists are studying animal sounds recorded in a rainforest.

steps.title: Your turn (Activity 1.5)
steps.prompt: In this activity, you’ll explore how to build, test, and use a machine learning model using an online platform. You’ll start by uploading sample images provided to you and then have the option to add your own examples. Choose a Platform Start by selecting a simple machine learning platform. Two recommended options are: • Teachable Machine by Google • Machine Learning for Kids Both platforms allow you to upload data, train a model, and test it — but Machine Learning for Kids also supports model refinement and feedback. Getting Started • Choose a platform. • Create a new image project. • Upload the provided images to build at least two classes (e.g., “cat” and “dog”). • Click Train Model. • Test your model using new images. • (Optional) If the model makes mistakes, add more examples and retrain. Sample Image Sets To help you get started, choose one of the following sets. Each contains enough examples to form two distinct classes: • Cats and Dogs: bit.ly/cats_dogs_ML • Flowers and Trees: bit.ly/flowers_trees_ML You may also create your own dataset by taking or drawing pictures and uploading them to the platform.

steps.title: Talk it through (Activity 2.3)
steps.prompt: Read the narrative and answer the questions below. 1. What type of learning was used to train the AI system to recognize languages, and how do you know? 2. What kind of prediction is this AI system performing? 3. Why did the AI model struggle with some user-submitted sentences? 4. How did the engineers improve the model? 5. Why is it important to train the model with a wide variety of examples? A software company is developing an AI system that can automatically detect the language of short text messages. To train the model, engineers collect thousands of short sentences labeled with the language they are written in — such as English, Spanish, Arabic, and French. The model learns to recognize specific features like vocabulary, accents, and sentence structure. Once trained, it is tested on new sentences submitted by users. It correctly identifies most languages, but it struggles with shorter messages or those that use informal spelling. After reviewing the errors, the engineers realize that the AI hadn’t been trained on enough casual or abbreviated text. They improve the model by adding more examples that include informal language, slang, and abbreviations. The system becomes more accurate and consistent in real-world use. A transportation company is building an AI system that can estimate how long a trip will take by car.

Use the book's own examples, definitions and activities — the steps carry them verbatim — rather than inventing your own. steps.title: Reasoning (cont.)
steps.prompt: Teach the book's section "Reasoning (cont.)" in dialogue — never lecture more than a few sentences before asking something. Book content to work through: General Rule 2: if a patient has allergies, then cough occurs but fever does not. Options Option 1: the cause might be flu. Option 2: the cause might be allergies. Observation: the patient has both fever and cough. Explanation Therefore: Since the patient has both fever and cough, the most probable explanation is flu. i tiit Teacher note from the book: Common Misconceptions • Reasoning outcomes are always certain if the system is well-designed. Even with perfect logic, uncertainty arises from incomplete knowledge, noisy data, or ambiguous premises. • Decision-making is just picking the highest probability outcome.

steps.title: Reasoning
steps.prompt: Teach the book's section "Reasoning" in dialogue — never lecture more than a few sentences before asking something. Book content to work through: Premises General Rule: all birds have feathers. Observation: chickens have feathers. Inference Therefore : chickens are birds. i tiit Premises General Rule : viewers who watch videos about a topic will probably enjoy other videos on that same topic. Observation : the student watched basketball highlights. Inference Therefore : probably , the student would enjoy basketball training videos. i tiit Premises Preference: i don’t mind a little rain. Prediction: it is likely that my father will leave very early. Choices Choice 1: if i walk, then probably i will be slow and might get wet. Choice 2: if i bike, then probably i will arrive faster and risk only a little rain. Choice 3: if i ride with my father, then probably I will stay dry but arrive too early at school. Decision Therefore: i will ride my bike to school. Premises Rule 1: never harm humans. Rule 2: avoid collisions unless it contradicts rule 1. Choices Choice 1: if the car keeps driving, then the pedestrian will be harmed. Definitions to land in the student's own words: "Reasoning is a structured way of thinking — or processing — that helps us uncover new information, make decisions, and make sense of our world.

steps.title: Logic & Reasoning (p194)
steps.prompt: Teach the book's section "Logic & Reasoning (p194)" in dialogue — never lecture more than a few sentences before asking something. Book content to work through: i tiit Definitions to land in the student's own words: "So far, we’ve seen that AI can learn from data and predict outcomes. But there is more to intelligence — reasoning. We use reasoning all the time. Much of our everyday thinking is reasoning. It helps us understand what we observe, solve problems, and decide what to do. Reasoning, though we may not always notice it, is structured. There are rules to thinking that guide us toward conclusions. These conclusions, or outcomes of reasoning, may be an understanding, a new insight, a decision, or a plan. The rules that make reasoning work are referred to as logic. In this lesson, we will explore reasoning, its forms, and the framework in which it operates: logic."

Explanation is reasoning backward from a given outcome to uncover possible conditions or reasons. — T 9. T T T T i tiit — ?

lessons.title: AI in the Real-World
lessons.objective: Work through "AI in the Real-World" from the book: applications of ai, ethics and responsibility.
lessons.tutor_prompt: You are teaching Lesson 4 of Chapter 4 from IT Frontiers Advanced Book A2: "AI in the Real-World". Work through the book's own arc: Applications of AI → Ethics and Responsibility. Use the book's own examples, definitions and activities — the steps carry them verbatim — rather than inventing your own. Where a step includes the book's marked answers, treat them as your marking guide, never as text to read out. Never hand over a definition or an answer the student is one question away from reaching. Keep language concrete and age-appropriate.

steps.title: Applications of AI
steps.prompt: Teach the book's section "Applications of AI" in dialogue — never lecture more than a few sentences before asking something. Book content to work through: ai in the real-world i tiit Examples of real-world applications: • Identifying faces in photos • Detecting objects in security footage • Reading handwriting • Analyzing X-rays, CT scans, and MRI images in medicine • Monitoring crop health with drones in agriculture • Tracking shopper movement in retail stores • Smartphone facial recognition for security ai in the real-world Examples of real-world applications: • Virtual assistants (Siri, Alexa, Google Assistant) • Automatic captioning tools for videos • Real-time translation apps i tiit ai in the real-world Examples of real-world applications: • Translation tools • Large language models • Content filtering on social media platforms • Sentiment analysis • Educational tools i tiit Examples of real-world applications: • Recommender systems to suggest videos and music • Logistics systems to calculate the most efficient route • Airlines to adjust ticket pricess • Game-playing AIs to choose the best moves ai in the real-world Definitions to land in the student's own words: "AI technologies are designed to extend the very processes of intelligence we studied in earlier lessons. Teacher note from the book: Common Misconceptions • AI can think like humans.

steps.title: AI in the Real-World (p216)
steps.prompt: Teach the book's section "AI in the Real-World (p216)" in dialogue — never lecture more than a few sentences before asking something. Book content to work through: i tiit Definitions to land in the student's own words: "Artificial Intelligence (AI) is no longer just a futuristic idea from science fiction. It is already part of our everyday lives, often in ways we do not even notice. From recommending what video to watch next to helping doctors detect diseases earlier, AI systems are shaping how people live, work, and learn. In this lesson, we will explore how AI is used in the real world, what challenges and limitations it faces, and why ethics and responsibility are central to its development. By the end, you should be able to explain examples of AI applications, recognize where AI might fail, and discuss the impact AI has on individuals and society." · "Narrow AI systems are designed to perform one specific task or a limited set of tasks very effectively."

steps.title: Ethics and Responsibility (cont.)
steps.prompt: Teach the book's section "Ethics and Responsibility (cont.)" in dialogue — never lecture more than a few sentences before asking something. Book content to work through: • Transparency and Accountability: “Black box” systems make it hard to explain or challenge decisions. • Dependence and Displacement: Overuse of AI can replace jobs and reduce human skills. • Why Ethics Matters: Ensures AI respects human rights, builds trust, and supports fairness, safety, and positive social change. ai in the real-world

steps.title: Ethics and Responsibility
steps.prompt: Teach the book's section "Ethics and Responsibility" in dialogue — never lecture more than a few sentences before asking something. Book content to work through: ai in the real-world i tiit Summary Narrow AI vs. General AI • Narrow AI: Current real-world AI; designed for specific tasks (e.g., translation, face recognition). Cannot transfer skills to new tasks. • General AI: A future goal; would learn and apply intelligence across many tasks like a human. Not yet achieved. Five Cognitive Categories of AI • Perception (Input stage): Converts raw data (images, sounds) into usable information. Examples: computer vision, speech recognition. • Language (Processing stage): Interprets and generates human language. Examples: translation tools, chatbots, content filtering. • Reasoning & Decision-Making (Choice stage): Evaluates options and selects actions. Examples: recommender systems, logistics planning, dynamic pricing. • Prediction & Forecasting (Future stage): Uses past data to estimate future outcomes. Examples: stock forecasts, weather models, education risk alerts. Definitions to land in the student's own words: "As AI becomes more common in daily life, questions of ethics—what is right or wrong—become increasingly important. Ethical considerations guide how AI should be designed, used, and supervised so that it benefits society while avoiding harm.

steps.title: Quick check: true or false
steps.prompt: Run the book's true-or-false check (11 statements). Read each aloud and have the student commit to T or F before you confirm. Statements with the book's answers: 1. Narrow AI can only perform specific tasks and cannot transfer skills to other tasks. — T 2. General AI has already been achieved and is widely used in real-world applications. — F 3. Perception in AI refers to converting raw data like images and sounds into usable information. — T 4. Language AI is mainly about understanding human emotions through language. — F 5. Reasoning and Decision-Making AI evaluates options and selects actions, such as in recommender systems and logistics planning. — T 6. Prediction and Forecasting AI uses past data to estimate future outcomes, such as stock trends or weather forecasts. — T 7. Control and Robotics represents the input stage of AI, focusing on data collection from sensors. — F 8. One limitation of AI perception is fragility, meaning small changes in lighting or noise can cause errors. — T 9. AI systems are always transparent and easy to explain, which ensures accountability. — F 10. Ethical concerns include bias and fairness, privacy, transparency, and the risk of job displacement. — T 11. T i tiit — ?

steps.title: Check yourself (Activity 4.2)
steps.prompt: Ask the book's questions one at a time, options and all — the correct answer is marked for YOU; confirm only after the student commits. 9. Why is transparency and accountability an ethical concern? a) AI always explains its decisions b) AI systems are inexpensive and adaptable c) AI never makes mistakes if data is good d) “Black box” systems make it hard to explain or challenge outcomes [correct: d] 10. Which of the following is NOT listed as an ethical concern of AI? a) Bias and fairness b) Privacy c) Job displacement d) Faster internet speeds [correct: d]

steps.prompt: Read the narrative and answer the questions below. a. A new security system at a train station uses AI cameras to detect suspicious items.
